content_of_post_to_comment: One of the major disagreements between Plato and, his student, Aristotle concerns whether “common sense” has any value. That’s a rough way of putting it. A more sophisticated way of saying this: Aristotle develops what we call the “endoxic method,” which means that the starting points of an intellectual inquiry should be what the wise have thought about something and/or what “the many” have thought about it. So, even the general populace’s thoughts should be taken into account. That doesn’t mean that the wise or the many are always right. But there is some kernel of truth in what the many believe or what the wise have taught. The way that expresses itself for Aristotle looks like this. When he writes his work on the soul, De Anima, he starts by surveying what his predecessors thought. When he writes his work on ethics, the Nicomachean Ethics, he starts by surveying what the many think. The many, for instance, think that the greatest good for humans is happiness. That’s a nice starting point. Aristotle is totally happy to judge these starting points as being wrong. But if they’re wrong, they’re wrong in a way that makes them be useful. They’re usefully wrong. That’s because they have some kernel of truth in them that makes them appealing to the wise or to the many. But much of the time, Aristotle doesn’t even really say that the starting points are wrong. With this in mind, Aristotle treats them as “reputable beliefs.” The Greek word for that is “endoxon.” Hence the name of this method: the endoxic method. This couldn’t be more different from Plato. Plato thought that it was so entirely possible that everyone is entirely wrong about a subject that we shouldn’t even consider what became Aristotle’s endoxic method. For Plato, the overwhelming majority of humanity, and maybe even everyone at any point in time, is groping around in the dark, looking for the truth. We don’t have any obvious, necessary connection to the truth. He’d look at Aristotle and not quite get why the endoxic method even occurs to him as a possibility. Why think that there is some kernel of truth in whatever the wise or the many have believed? But Aristotle is just so much more optimistic as a thinker. Our five senses clue us into the truth in a way that should inspire some confidence in our predecessors and contemporaries. Plato, meanwhile, had no confidence in our body’s senses at all.
